note_on_method: This is a state page, so almost everything on it is a claim about coverage rather than about a court. Where it describes a place, the source is that operator's own publication. Where it describes what is missing, it names the town we looked at and the reason we declined it, because 'not listed' and 'does not exist' are different things and a reader deserves to know which one they are looking at. This page was rewritten when Charlotte was added; the previous version said every verified court in the state was in one county, and listed Charlotte among the places we had not assessed. Nobody working on this has played on any court in North Carolina.

slots.coverage:
North Carolina has a hundred counties. This page covers two.

Twenty-four sites, 106 courts, four municipalities, two operators of quite different kinds. Wake County holds nineteen of those sites and 77 of the courts, split between three town parks departments: Raleigh with eleven parks and 44 courts, Apex with five facilities and 21, and Cary with three parks and 12. Mecklenburg County holds the other five sites and 29 courts, all inside Charlotte and all run by a single county-level department rather than by the city.

The bar is the same everywhere and worth restating: a venue publishes here when the organisation that runs it identifies its own courts in public. Not a listing site's count, not a number we inferred from a photograph or measured off a map — the operator's own record. What is striking, having now read a dozen North Carolina operators, is how many different ways they clear or miss that bar.

Raleigh states each location's count on one pickleball page and then states the citywide total in prose, and the parts add up to the whole. Apex publishes a table with a column each for indoor or outdoor, lights and court count, and then repeats most of those counts on the venue's own page. Cary states nothing centrally and everything locally, in the features list of each facility's page. And Mecklenburg County states no count at all — it lists individual numbered courts, split between the ones you can reserve and the ones that are always open play, so Charlotte's counts are the number of distinct court numbers the county names at each park. Four operators, four completely different publishing habits, all of them adequate.

The ones that are not adequate are more instructive, and we have now assessed five and declined them.

Durham publishes a proper tennis and pickleball page with two tables. The first lists twelve parks with their tennis court counts and a Yes or No for whether pickleball lines are painted on them. The second is headed Pickleball Court Information and contains exactly one row: Piney Wood Park, twelve courts, twelve lighted. So Durham states a count for one venue and a yes-or-no for four others, and a city page here needs three. Durham has more pickleball than Cary does. Cary publishes and Durham does not.

Winston-Salem is the mirror image, and the most frustrating of the five. Its official pickleball page carries a clean table of seven court locations — Crystal Towers, Little Creek Park, Oak Summit Park, Old Town Park, Reynolds Park, Sedge Garden Park and Shaffner Park — with a full street address and postcode for every one. Seven venues, seven addresses, and not a single court count. It is exactly the data Durham lacks, missing exactly the data Durham has.

Greensboro names three parks with outdoor courts — Smith Community Park, Woodlea Park and Lake Daniel Park — open dawn until dusk, plus indoor courts at the Greensboro Sportsplex at $5 a drop-in. No counts and no addresses. Holly Springs states four outdoor courts at the North Main Athletic Complex and indoor open play at the W.E. Hunt Center with "up to three nets", which is one countable venue where three are needed. And Wake Forest reconciles beautifully at 18 active courts across named facilities, but three of its four entries are at Flaherty Park, so counting them as three venues to clear a three-venue threshold would be meeting the letter of the rule by breaking its point.

Then there is everywhere we have not looked at all: Fayetteville, Wilmington, Asheville, Chapel Hill, Concord, Gastonia, High Point, Jacksonville, Rocky Mount. Their absence carries no information about their courts. It is a statement about our reading list.
slots.seasonality:
The honest headline is that we cannot tell you much about North Carolina weather from a source, and we are not going to tell you about it from memory.

What operators publish, when they publish it, is the two things that actually decide whether a court is usable outside a summer afternoon: whether it is lit, and whether there is anywhere indoors to go. And the first of those now splits the state neatly in two.

Raleigh and Apex both state lighting for every single location. Nine of Raleigh's eleven are lit, on a timer to 10 p.m.; Fred Fletcher Park and Southgate Park are marked unlit and are daylight-only. Four of Apex's five are lit, three of them running 6:30 a.m. to 10 p.m. year round. Cary states it for one of its three. Mecklenburg County states it for none of its five — there is no lighting information anywhere on its courts page, so all 29 Charlotte courts read "Not verified yet" on this site. That is a gap in publishing rather than evidence of darkness, but it means that for more than a quarter of the verified courts in this state we cannot answer the single most seasonal question there is.

Where lighting is stated, the most useful fact is an inversion. The largest pickleball site in Apex is Pleasant Park, with six courts, and it is the one unlit site in that town: its published court hours are "Sunrise to 30 minutes after Sunset". So from November to February the biggest concentration of courts in Apex shuts in mid-afternoon while the smaller lit sites run for another six hours. Plan a winter evening around court count and you will drive to the wrong park.

Indoors, the verified picture is close to bare and the real one is not. There are exactly four verified indoor pickleball courts in North Carolina on this site, all at the John M. Brown Community Center in Apex, restricted to players aged 55 and over during designated open gym hours. That is not because indoor pickleball is rare here. It is because indoor programmes are published as programmes rather than as facilities. Raleigh Parks runs indoor open play at thirteen community centres at $3 a session or $15 for a four-month pass, with nets and balls provided, and publishes no court count for any of the thirteen gyms. Cary rents three indoor courts at Middle Creek Community Center at $10 an hour on a timetable that changes with the season — Thursday and Friday afternoons and Saturday lunchtimes from March to October, shorter hours from November to February — and publishes no street address for the building. Greensboro runs indoor drop-in at its Sportsplex, Monday to Friday 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., at $5 or $30 for a ten-visit card. Durham, Holly Springs and Winston-Salem all run indoor sessions too.

So what we can source about seasonality here is that the operators themselves treat winter as a separate problem: they run indoor sessions on winter schedules, they light most outdoor courts to 10 p.m. where they light them at all, and one town has built its largest site without lights. What we cannot source, and will not invent, is anything about summer heat, humidity, thunderstorm closures or what these surfaces are like in August. No North Carolina operator we have read publishes a weather closure policy for a pickleball court, and until one does this section stays short on purpose.
slots.notable:
A directory that lists everything equally is not much use, so here is what is genuinely distinctive in the verified North Carolina set — including one venue that is notable precisely because it is missing.

Sanderford Road Park in south-east Raleigh is the largest verified pickleball site in the state: ten permanent courts, all lit. That is nearly a quarter of Raleigh's 44 courts on one site, and more than the whole of Cary's verified provision. It is one of only three Raleigh locations the city describes as permanent pickleball courts rather than lines painted over tennis.

Clarks Creek Park in north Charlotte is the second largest at eight, and it is the best place in the state to turn up without a booking — three of its eight courts are permanently open play, more than any other park in Mecklenburg County keeps back.

The John M. Brown Community Center in Apex holds the only verified indoor pickleball courts in North Carolina, and at the time of writing the only ones anywhere in this directory. Four of them, marked Indoor and lit in the town's own table, available only for ages 55 and over during designated open gym hours. If you are under 55 this is not a venue, it is a fact about the state.

Pleasant Park in Apex does something no other operator here does: it publishes live court occupancy, so you can see whether its six courts are busy before you get in the car. Given that the same park has no lights and closes thirty minutes after sunset, the combination is oddly characteristic — genuinely modern in one respect and plainly limited in another.

Freedom Park in Charlotte is worth a paragraph for its numbering. Its pickleball courts are numbered 11 to 16 because courts 1 to 10 at the same park are tennis, listed separately on the same page. Mecklenburg runs one series across both sports at that site rather than restarting it, so you can read the history of the conversion straight out of the court numbers.

Baileywick Park in north Raleigh is the only place in the verified set with covered courts — its page lists Court A as covered and Court B as covered centre, and schedules pickleball on both. Two cautions travel with that: Court A was closed for repairs when we last checked with no reopening date, and Baileywick is the venue where Raleigh's own two inventories disagree, the pickleball page saying six courts and the city's GIS layer four.

And the notable absence: Cary Tennis Park. The town states it has four lighted pickleball courts. It is the best-known racquet facility in the region, it has 32 championship tennis courts including seven covered, and it hosts the Professional Pickleball Association tour. It appears nowhere on this site, because across its facility page, its pickleball page and its court reservations page the Town of Cary prints no street address for it. That rule costs us the most famous pickleball venue in North Carolina, which is the point of having it: a rule you suspend when it is expensive is not a rule.
slots.growth:
North Carolina is a good place to watch pickleball provision change, because one town has published its own history in enough detail to read the pattern — including the parts most operators quietly leave out.

Wake Forest has published a dated timeline. It begins in 2009 with pickleball on one chalked tennis court. In 2013 a group of citizens approached the town asking for space, initially only that lines be taped on a gym floor. In 2014 the town resurfaced the Flaherty Park tennis courts and added eight pickleball courts to them for shared use, and installed four at Wake Forest Middle School. In 2015 it resurfaced the tennis courts at Heritage High School and installed six shared-use courts, and partnered with a seminary for temporary courts in a gymnasium. In 2016 it replaced the gym floor at Flaherty Park Community Center and added three courts to it. In 2017 it opened the Flaherty Park Pickleball Courts — four outdoor, lighted and dedicated, the first in the town built for the game rather than borrowed from another one. In 2019 it added three more at the new Joyner Park Community Center. In 2021 it was approached about building a pickleball complex, and in 2022 a $24.4 million parks and recreation bond passed, including a Multipurpose Sports Complex to house dedicated pickleball courts.

Tape on a gym floor, then lines on tennis courts, then a small dedicated block, then a bond-funded complex. Every town in this state seems to be somewhere along that arc.

But the more valuable part of Wake Forest's timeline is the subtraction. The four courts at Wake Forest Middle School are, in the town's own words, no longer in use. The six at Heritage High School were removed once the dedicated courts were installed. The town states it has installed 32 courts since 2013 and currently offers 18 active ones, which means roughly nine of every seventeen courts it has ever built are gone. No directory publishes that. Court counts on listing sites only ever go up, because nobody edits a listing to remove something. A town that tells you what it took away is telling you what the shared-use arrangements were actually like to play on.

The same conversion shows in the towns we publish, once you know to look for it. In Raleigh, 22 of the 44 outdoor courts are permanent pickleball courts at three sites and the other 22 are lines painted over tennis at six parks, over basketball at Southgate and over shared hard courts at Baileywick — an even split between purpose-built and borrowed. In Charlotte the evidence is in the numbering: Freedom Park's pickleball courts start at 11 because ten tennis courts came first. In Cary, Ed Yerha Park is the town's designated home of outdoor pickleball and was formerly White Oak Park, renamed for a councilmember who served from 2012 to 2022, and the town's open data still carries the old name on the same map point. In Apex, Pleasant Park is the newest park in the town and carries its largest block of courts.

What is under way right now is smaller and more concrete. Raleigh began a lighting upgrade at North Hills Park on 24 August 2026, closing the courts; daytime play reopened on 2 September with completion targeted for 8 September. Baileywick Park's Pavilion-Court A was closed for repairs on 24 August 2026 with no reopening date. And twelve courts in Charlotte are waiting on a definition rather than on construction: Mecklenburg County lists six "hybrid" courts each at Latta Park and Tuckaseegee Park under a heading it never explains.

The honest summary is that North Carolina's public pickleball is roughly half converted tennis and basketball surfaces and half purpose-built courts, that the purpose-built share is growing, that at least one town has a bond-funded complex coming, and that the true statewide count is a moving number nobody publishes. We can tell you 106 courts across twenty-four verified sites in four towns, checked on 3 September 2026. We cannot tell you what North Carolina has, and neither can anyone else who is being careful.

faqs.q: How many pickleball courts are there in North Carolina?
faqs.a: Nobody knows, including us, and anyone who gives you a single number for the state is guessing. We have verified 106 courts across twenty-four sites in four towns — Raleigh, Charlotte, Apex and Cary — where each count came from the organisation that runs the courts. North Carolina has a hundred counties and we have verified venues in two of them. The number on this page is a floor with a citation, not an estimate of the total.

faqs.q: Why does this page cover only two counties?
faqs.a: Because that is where we have got to, and because most operators do not publish what a venue page needs. Wake County came first because Raleigh's parks department publishes a court count for every location and a citywide total that reconciles with them; Cary and Apex followed. Mecklenburg County came next because it identifies every court individually by number. Five other North Carolina towns have been assessed and declined, each for a specific reason set out above.

faqs.q: Why isn't Durham here? It has more courts than Cary.
faqs.a: It does, and it is not here anyway. Durham Parks and Recreation publishes a Pickleball Court Information table with exactly one row in it: Piney Wood Park, twelve courts, twelve lighted. Its other pickleball is recorded as a Yes in a column on the tennis court table, which tells you lines exist without telling you how many courts they make. A city needs three venues with identified courts to publish here, and Durham gives one.

Winston-Salem is the most frustrating near-miss in the state. Its official pickleball page lists seven court locations with a full street address and postcode for every one — Crystal Towers, Little Creek Park, Oak Summit Park, Old Town Park, Reynolds Park, Sedge Garden Park and Shaffner Park — and gives no court count for any of them. It has precisely the data Durham lacks and lacks precisely the data Durham has. One column would publish seven venues.

faqs.q: Where can I play indoors in North Carolina?
faqs.a: There are four verified indoor courts in the state, all at the John M. Brown Community Center in Apex, for players aged 55 and over during designated open gym hours. That is the verified part, not the whole scene. Raleigh runs indoor open play at thirteen community centres at $3 a session or $15 for four months; Cary rents three indoor courts at Middle Creek at $10 an hour; Greensboro runs indoor drop-in at its Sportsplex at $5. None of those publishes what a venue page needs — a court count and an address — so none appears as a venue.

faqs.q: What is the biggest pickleball site in the state?
faqs.a: Of what we have verified, Sanderford Road Park in south-east Raleigh: ten permanent lit courts on one site. Clarks Creek Park in north Charlotte follows with eight. Then a cluster of sixes — Method Community Park, North Hills Park and Baileywick Park in Raleigh, McCrimmon Park in Cary, Pleasant Park in Apex, and Clanton, Freedom and Martin Luther King Jr. Park in Charlotte.

faqs.q: Which courts can I actually book?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on the operator, and Charlotte is the clearest. Mecklenburg County marks nineteen of its 29 courts reservable for "a small fee" and keeps ten permanently open play, naming which numbered courts fall on each side and always leaving some back at every park. Raleigh marks Method and North Hills drop-in only and offers a reservation form elsewhere. Apex forbids booking outright — its ordinance bars organised league play and private lessons outside town programming. Cary's three park sites are all first-come, first-served.

faqs.q: Is pickleball still growing in North Carolina?
faqs.a: On the published evidence, yes, and it is changing shape as it grows. The arc visible in Wake Forest's own timeline — taped lines on a gym floor, then lines painted over tennis, then a small block of dedicated courts, then a bond-funded complex — is the one these towns seem to follow. Wake Forest's 2022 parks bond of $24.4 million includes a Multipurpose Sports Complex for dedicated pickleball. What is less often reported is the subtraction: the same town states it installed 32 courts since 2013 and has 18 active today, having removed the school courts once dedicated ones existed.

faqs.q: How do you decide which North Carolina town to add next?
faqs.a: By whether its operator identifies its own courts, for at least three separate sites. Not by population, and not by how much pickleball a listing site claims is there. That is why this page covers Apex, population around seventy thousand, alongside Charlotte. Towns already assessed and declined are named above with the reason, so you can disagree with a specific judgement rather than with a silence.
